headings: # Before You Try to Go Deep: from the depth paragraphs (map change: AMEND.IC.CONTINUITY_TITRATION, #126)
intro: Left to the AI guide: the no to inner-child work (you cut depth draft 1, and "Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too" in When to Change the Strategy covers the reader's side), and the pause bookkeeping ("observable change—plus your own agreement").

rows.label: T1
rows.after: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now?
rows.text: If a depth is too much, go gentler instead of pushing through with one technique after another, and instead of giving up on your little one.
source: If you do want the relationship but a particular depth
That means turning the depth down
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.

In the article already, partly: "leave the deeper conversation until later" (the paragraph before) and "change course sooner (stopping counts)". New: going shallower, and not hopping between techniques.

rows.label: T2
rows.text: If you can't stop and come back, or going inward is making it worse, come back out to the room first. Later, a gentle way back in is one protective thing in your life, or a short eyes-open hello before any imagery.
source: If you do want the relationship but a particular depth
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.

rows.label: T3
rows.text: If you take a full break from your little one, note why and how far you'd got, and come back at or below that when you want to.
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.

headings: ## Your Body Might Need Some Love First: from the pleasantness paragraphs (map change: AMEND.IC.SCAFFOLDED_CHALLENGE, #126)

rows.label: T4
rows.after: When your nervous system is flooded
rows.text: How pleasant a session felt doesn't tell you whether it was too much. Hard isn't harm, and staying present isn't enough by itself.
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.
In the article already, partly: intense isn't progress ("I could have kept crying forever."). Your embedded map post sits between the paragraph before and this.

rows.label: T5
rows.text: What tells you more: the next few days (sleep, getting through the day), whether you want to go back toward it, and whether it felt hard but workable or just too much.
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.

rows.label: T6
rows.text: If you can't tell yet, don't call it healing or harm. Make the next one a bit easier, one change at a time. If you're getting worse, change several things and get support. Bring the challenge back gradually.
source: If those answers are not known yet
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.

rows.label: T7
rows.text: Dreams and images show what feels important or needed now. They aren't evidence that something happened, and they shouldn't be used to build a memory.
source: Dreams and imagery can be useful
notes: A teaching point: what a reader needs from the guide paragraph, in one or two plain sentences. Not article prose; tick it and I draft it.

In the article already, partly: "Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn't prove they happened." (said for an altered state). The difficult-dream paragraph of a later section goes with this one.
